title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Welcome & framing
Hurricanes, Katrina & Health
Ecosystems ↔︎ infrastructure ↔︎ people

Set the session arc: 1) hurricane physics vs. impacts, 2) Katrina as environmental justice case, 3) health systems & preparedness, 4) designing better risk communication than “category only”.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Roadmap

Hurricane basics (multi-hazard, not just wind)

Category vs. consequence

Climate change & rapid intensification

Modeling, AI & data gaps

Katrina: infrastructure, justice, and health

Preparedness & community capacity

Discussion & applications


Emphasize synthesis over recall. We’ll connect to prior units: redlining, weather attribution, and extreme events & health.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
What a hurricane is (and isn’t)


Warm-core, low-pressure tropical cyclones with organized rotation





Hurricane Hazards



Wind


Storm surge


Rain


Tornadoes










Podcast: “warm core” due to latent heat release; strongest winds near surface. Frame risk as Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Names across basins

Hurricanes (N. Atlantic, E. North Pacific)

Typhoons (W. North Pacific)

Cyclones (Indian Ocean, S. Hemisphere)


Measurement conventions differ (1-min vs 10-min sustained winds). Useful caveat when reading global studies or WHO briefs.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
section: Why storms don’t cross the equator
text:
Why storms don’t cross the equator
Insufficient Coriolis (spin) near 0° latitude

Quick think-pair: other rotation-dependent features (trade winds, Hadley cells, gyres). Bring it back in 2 minutes.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Early-season quiet: Saharan Air Layer
Dry, dusty air → suppresses Atlantic development
Bonus: nutrient delivery to Amazon soils

Teleconnections matter: the same dust that dims storms can fertilize ecosystems. Great “systems thinking” example.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Saffir–Simpson: helpful, but narrow
Categories are wind-only → underplay surge/rain risks

Tie to Harvey/Imelda examples from podcast: lower categories can still be catastrophic via flooding. Set up later redesign activity.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Weakening ≠ safe
A weakening hurricane can expand → bigger wind/surge footprint

Public messaging risk: people anchor to the number, not the footprint. Previews Katrina dynamics at landfall.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Rapid Intensification (RI)

More frequent near landfall

Compressed decision windows for evacuation & hospitals


Prompt: If you run a coastal hospital, which actions move from T-48h to T-72h under higher RI risk? (Dialysis scheduling, O2 logistics, early discharges, staff lodging.)

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Modeling today
Physics-based NWP + data assimilation (balloons, aircraft, satellites)
Emerging AI track/intensity guidance → hybrid future

Key point: AI complements physics; data gaps (e.g., fewer radiosondes) degrade both. Funding = forecast skill = public health outcomes.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Interlude video
(Swap in a short eye/eyewall or surge explainer clip)

Keep it to 3–4 minutes. Ask them to identify the hazard chain they see: wind → surge → infrastructure failure → health outcomes.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Image: anatomy of a cyclone

placeholder
Narrate inflow/outflow, eyewall, rainbands, and where hazards concentrate relative to track.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Case study: Hurricane Katrina (2005)




What made this a particularly devestating disaster?



Get into groups of 2-4 and create a list of the top 3 contributing factors.

Be prepared to explain the spatial/temporal and the social/economic context mediating each factor.

Return to discuss as a group






Stress that many deaths were from post-landfall flooding, not peak winds. Infrastructure failure + social vulnerability → health catastrophe.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Katrina & environmental justice





How did the legacy of redlining contribute to the impacts?


Low-elevation, levee-adjacent neighborhoods, Car access & evacuation ability, Disproportionate impact in Lower Ninth/St. Bernard





Connect to previous class: how historical housing policy maps onto present-day disaster risk and health inequities.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Public health cascades
Acute: drowning, trauma, CO poisoning
Subacute: waterborne disease, mold, asthma
Chronic: PTSD/depression, DV rise, displacement

Introduce disaster epidemiology terms (excess mortality, indirect deaths, syndemics). Ask: What surveillance would you deploy at 1 week / 1 month?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Evacuation paradox: Hurricane Rita (2005)

Mass evacuation → heat, dehydration, traffic mortality


Rita saw >2.5M evacuees; >50% of deaths occurred during evacuation. Discussion: When is shelter-in-place safer, and how do we message that?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Communication that helps
Local trusted mets (hype-free)
Translate cones/probabilities to actions
Waffle House Index as on-the-ground proxy

120-char exercise: Draft a text for a coastal ZIP under 48-hr TS warning with high surge risk (who/what/when/where).

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Katrina lessons for today

Category ≠ consequence

Community capacity drives mortality trajectory

Mitigation is equity-positive public health policy


Bridge to ROI and planning: “Mitigation Saves” (~$6 per $1). Ask which two investments (grey/green or social) they’d prioritize now for NOLA.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Background image placeholder

Use a powerful image (levees, surge, shelters). Let it breathe, then solicit 2 reflections before moving on.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Preparedness across scales
Household ↔︎ neighborhood ↔︎ clinic/hospital ↔︎ city

We’ll ladder through: home kits & meds, neighbor check-ins, clinic surge, municipal transit/shelter ops. Assign a brief preparedness plan later.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Household & neighborhood

Redundant alerts; meds & docs ready

Know your floodplain / drainage

Pets, caregivers, carpool networks, mutual aid


Quick activity: sketch a neighbor check-in grid (names, needs, contact, “last seen”).

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Clinics & hospitals

Pre-position oxygen/dialysis/insulin; backup power

On-site staff lodging & childcare

Early discharges; telehealth triage

Post-storm: heat, mold, vector control


Mini-scenario: A Cat 2 is forecast to RI to Cat 4 in 24–36h. What activates at T-36h, T-12h, and +48h?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Community & policy levers

Cool roofs, raised utilities, permeable streets

Surge barriers, wetland restoration, buyouts

Transit-enabled evacuation

Fund local EM; measure outcomes


Highlight co-benefits (air quality, heat). Note who benefits first if budgets are tight; link to equity.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Video: policy or health case
(Paste a short YouTube explainer; adjust for autoplay per your policy.)

Prompt: list three “no-regret” investments with health benefits even absent a storm next year.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Designing better risk metrics
Beyond category: surge, rainfall, footprint, RI risk
Exposure: population, assets, hospitals
Vulnerability: SVI, car access, language, disability

Group task (5–6 min): Propose a 4-component index for your chosen coastal city. One team shares out.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Quick attribution sidebar

Event attribution: probability & intensity shifting

Communicate as probabilistic, not deterministic


Use the “loaded dice” metaphor; avoid over-claiming single-cause narratives.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Takeaways

Hazard ↔︎ exposure ↔︎ vulnerability → health

Category is not destiny; context rules

Mitigation + justice are core public health strategies


Ask for 1-minute reflections: “One action I’ll advocate locally is…”

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Next steps

Add local flood maps, shelters, bus routes

Invite clinic/EM partners for a tabletop

Optional: 2-page Preparedness Plan with equity focus


Offer extra credit for community engagement (e.g., helping a neighbor build a kit or mapping a shelter route).

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Today’s roadmap

Hurricane basics (what they are / aren’t)
From category to consequences
Climate change & rapid intensification
Modeling, AI & funding realities
Katrina: infrastructure, justice, and health
Preparedness & community resilience
Discussion & applications


Flag that we’ll emphasize application & synthesis more than memorization. Encourage students to annotate 2–3 insights they can use in their ICP/PVA or health risk frameworks.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Hurricane ≠ just wind

Warm-core cyclones; low-pressure centers
Multi-hazard: wind + storm surge + rain + tornadoes
Impacts shaped by exposure, vulnerability, capacity


Podcast points: Saffir–Simpson is wind-only; underplays flooding/surge. Emphasize that risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability. Tie to environmental health determinants.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
A global vocabulary

Hurricanes (N. Atlantic, E. North Pacific)
Typhoons (W. North Pacific)
Cyclones (Indian Ocean, S. Hemisphere)


Clarify naming differences & measurement conventions (1-min vs 10-min sustained winds). Useful when reading global literature and surveillance reports.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
section: Why they don’t cross the equator
text:
Why they don’t cross the equator

Need Coriolis to sustain rotation
Insufficient spin near 0° latitude


Invite quick think-pair-share: What other Earth system features depend on rotation? (Trade winds, Hadley cells, ocean gyres.)

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Early-season dust & quiet periods
Saharan Air Layer: dry, dusty air → suppresses Atlantic development
Also fertilizes the Amazon with nutrients

Contrast “seed vs suppress” narratives; here dust is a suppressor of early-season storms while still part of a planetary teleconnection benefiting ecosystems.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Saffir–Simpson: useful but limited

Categories = wind speed only
Public perception: “Only a Cat 1” ⇒ under-prep
Flood, surge, compound hazards often dominate harm


Use Harvey (flooding), Imelda (tropical storm but huge rain) as examples. Ask: what alternative indicators would help communities decide?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
From physics to people

A weakening storm can grow in size, expanding the footprint of damaging winds & surge.


This nuance matters for evacuation timing and health system surge planning. We’ll revisit when we get to Katrina’s landfall dynamics.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Rapid intensification (RI)

Increasingly frequent near landfall
Compresses decision windows for evacuation & hospitals
Warmer SSTs + conducive atmospheric conditions


Prompt: If you manage a hospital on the coast, what 48–72 hr protocols change under higher RI risk? (Dialysis scheduling, oxygen logistics, early discharges, staff housing.)

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Modeling, AI & data

Physics-based models + data assimilation (balloons, aircraft, satellites)
New AI models: fast track guidance ⇒ hybrid future
Data gaps (e.g., fewer balloon launches) degrade forecasts


Emphasize “hybrid”: AI complements, not replaces, physics. Funding/staffing cuts propagate to forecast skill and thus public health outcomes.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Funding and institutions

NOAA/NWS staffing & research matter
Mitigation ROI: ~$6 saved for every $1 invested
Weather risk is bipartisan; budgets shape outcomes


Tie to policy literacy: how line items become lives saved. Connect to students’ local EM budgets and grant programs (BRIC, HMGP).

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Katrina: timeline & geography

Rapid escalation in Gulf
Landfall region & track overview
Levee breaches → 80% of New Orleans flooded


Emphasize failure of structural defenses; many fatalities occurred after peak winds due to flooding and delayed rescue.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Infrastructure & environmental justice

Aging levees, canals, subsidence, wetland loss
Redlining & disinvestment shaped who was at risk
Disparate impacts in Lower Ninth Ward & St. Bernard Parish


Connect to prior class on redlining: land value, elevation, building codes, and access to cars predict evacuation ability. Ask: Where would you map cooling centers/shelters?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Public health cascades

Acute: drowning, trauma, carbon monoxide poisoning
Subacute: waterborne disease, mold, asthma exacerbations
Chronic: mental health (PTSD, depression), domestic violence, displacement


Use disaster epidemiology terms: excess mortality, indirect deaths, syndemics, social determinants. Compare to heat waves & wildfire smoke.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Evacuation & counterexamples (Rita)

Rita (2005): >2.5M evacuees; >50% of deaths during evacuation
Heat, dehydration, traffic → health risks en route


Discussion: When is shelter-in-place safer than evacuation? How should messaging incorporate transportation & heat risks?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Communication that works

Local, trusted meteorologists (hype-free)
Translate cones & probabilistic info to action
The (legendary) Waffle House Index as a proxy


Exercise: Draft a 120-character text alert balancing urgency and specificity for a coastal zip code under a 48-hr tropical storm warning with high surge risk.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Katrina: lessons for today

Category ≠ consequence
Community capacity sets mortality trajectory
Pre-disaster mitigation pays off (and is equitable policy)


Prompt: Which two investments (infrastructure or social services) would you prioritize today for New Orleans? Justify with expected health benefits.

Redundancy in alerts; meds & documentation ready
Know your floodplain and drainage
Pet & caregiver plans; carpool networks; mutual aid


Assign: Students sketch a 2-page family comms plan + a neighbor check-in grid for their real residence.

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Clinics & hospitals

Pre-position oxygen, dialysis, insulin; backup power
Staffing: on-site lodging & daycare
Discharge acceleration & telehealth triage
Heat, mold, and vector control in aftermath


Mini-scenario: A Cat 2 is forecast to RI to Cat 4 within 24–36 hrs. What do you activate now vs 12 hrs vs post-landfall?

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes

Community & policy

Cool roofs, raised utilities, permeable surfaces
Surge barriers, wetland restoration, buyouts
Invest in public transit evacuation
Fund local EM; measure outcomes


Link back to mitigation ROI and co-benefits (air quality, heat relief).

title: Natural Disasters: Hurricanes
text:
Ecology & health

Displaced wildlife, altered vector ranges
Mold blooms, degraded indoor air
Water quality: sewage overflows, chemical releases


Tie to One Health. Ask: how would you monitor post-storm water and indoor air in schools?

Let this run; encourage examples from students’ hometowns or field sites.

title: Natural Disasters: Wildfires
text:
Air Quality & Smoke


Fine particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10)

deep lung penetration, systemic inflammation.






Gases

carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen oxides, volatile organics.






Sensitive populations

children, older adults, pregnant individuals, people with chronic lung/heart disease






Geographic spread

smoke plumes travel hundreds–thousands of miles → health impacts far beyond burn zone





External slides

title: Natural Disasters: Wildfires
text:
Water, Soil & Food Systems


Water contamination

Ash and debris runoff into reservoirs, rivers, groundwater.


Chemicals from burned infrastructure (plastics, metals).






Soil erosion

downstream flooding, sediment loads.






Food insecurity

if agricultural areas burn (loss of crops, livestock, pasture).

title: Natural Disasters: Wildfires
text:
Infrastructure & Access to Care


Healthcare disruption

clinics, hospitals evacuated/damaged; staff displaced.






Power outages

loss of refrigeration for medications, oxygen concentrators, dialysis.






Transportation blockages

hinder access to emergency care.






Shelter quality

overcrowding, poor ventilation, increased risk of infectious disease.
